description:
FILED s473t5f (#1501 round 7, uni/, 2026-09-13).  TWO halves, both
PRE-EXISTING, both measured; they share one file and are filed together only
because the round's ID range ended here.  A future session should split them.

================ HALF (a): perl's IDENTIFIER-START rule is not enforced ======

perl decides a length-1 variable name by `\p{_Perl_IDStart}`: anything else is
a COMPILE-TIME "Unrecognized character \x{...}; marked by <-- HERE ...".  PCL
either accepts it silently or raises its own differently-shaped refusal:

  code point              perl                        PCL
  U+0100 (IDStart)        accepted                    accepted
  U+3042 (IDStart)        accepted                    accepted
  U+0300 (combining)      Unrecognized character      ACCEPTED, no error
  U+2000 (space)          Unrecognized character      "Parser2 TODO:
                                                       unsupported declaration"
  U+E4ED (private use)    Unrecognized character      "PCL: cannot parse
                                                       (inline code): PPI
                                                       failed to tokenize it"
  U+0BE6 (Tamil digit 0)  Unrecognized character      same PPI refusal

AND THE SAME PROBE FOUND A SECOND LAYER, which is the DOMINANT one for the
live rows: **`\p{_Perl_IDStart}` itself answers NO for every character in
PCL**, U+0100 and U+3042 included -- cl-ppcre has no such property.  That is
#1036's property half.  t/uni/variables.t's big loop is

    if ( $chr =~ /^\p{_Perl_IDStart}$/ ) { is($@, '', "... works") }
    else { like($@, qr/\QUnrecognized character \x{$esc};/, "... illegal") }

so PCL always takes the ELSE branch and then asserts a diagnostic it does not
produce: both facts fire on the same row, and the property is what chooses the
wrong branch.  ~58,700 of the file's rows are this.

================ HALF (b): a ~60k-STRING-EVAL WALL ==========================

`t/uni/variables.t` makes 66,880 assertions, almost all a string eval, and PCL
compiles each one.  Measured:

    --timeout  90   1,248 ok / 27,934 not ok  = 29,182 rows
    --timeout 900   1,248 ok / 58,668 not ok  = 59,916 rows
    --timeout 900   1,248 ok / 58,668 not ok  = 59,916 rows   (the #366 serial
                                                               re-run: IDENTICAL)

Two runs at 900 s stopping at EXACTLY the same row is not a clock cut: the
process is still burning CPU and producing nothing.  The last row is
`\x{e4ec}`, so the wall is at code point U+E4ED -- and that code point
evaluates in 0 s on its own (probe evalrate5.pl, U+E4E8..U+E4F8 all 0 s), so
the wall is CUMULATIVE, not per-item.  An isolated 3,000-eval loop of the same
shape runs at ~270 evals/s, linear (3 s / 2 s / 1 s / 2 s / 1 s per 500), with
or without a TAP row per eval -- so nothing about the shape is slow; it is the
ACCUMULATION of ~60,000 distinct compiled evals in one image.

WHERE TO LOOK: the string-eval cache (every distinct eval TEXT is keyed and
kept -- see #296-B1 for what the key carries) plus SBCL's compiler heap.  The
cheap discriminating measurement is a bare loop of N distinct string evals
with `(room)` / `sb-ext:get-bytes-consed` sampled every 5,000: if the wall is
the cache, evicting it (or not caching a text seen once) moves the wall; if it
is the heap, the process is GC-thrashing and `--dynamic-space-size` moves it
(the #1590 family).

NO TIMEOUTS.TSV ALLOWANCE, and that is a decision, not an omission: the
registry promises "give the file the time and it finishes" and this file never
does, while 15 extra minutes per companion run would buy 30,734 more failing
rows of half (a) -- one already-named fact.  The file stays TIMEOUT with its
blessed 1,248/27,934, and its `baselines/row-shortfall.tsv` row now carries
this cause instead of UNEXPLAINED.

THE FILE'S THIRD FACT is already registered and is NOT part of this task: its
one aborted form is `"\x{11_1111}"`, the ruled refusal in
`docs/not-supported.md` "Code points above U+10FFFF (perl's extended UTF-8)"
(#419 / DECIDED Â§s422), which costs the enclosing 9-row loop.
